question: A 3-year-old malnourished child is brought to clinic with 6 weeks of low-grade fever and weight loss. His father was diagnosed with pulmonary TB 3 months ago. Which of the following best explains why children under 5 years are at higher risk for progressive primary TB disease compared to older children?

answers.text: They have a higher BCG coverage rate that paradoxically increases susceptibility

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. BCG vaccination provides protection, particularly against severe disseminated forms. It does not increase susceptibility.

answers.text: Their immature cell-mediated immunity cannot effectively contain the primary complex, allowing progression to active disease

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Children under 5 years have immature cell-mediated immunity, making them unable to effectively contain the primary Ghon focus. Combined with malnutrition and close contact (as here), this explains rapid progression from primary infection to active disease.

answers.text: They produce more sputum, making them more contagious and thus more exposed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Children are paucibacillary — they produce less sputum, not more. This actually makes them less contagious than adults.

answers.text: The TST Mantoux reaction is stronger in younger children, indicating greater bacterial load

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Mantoux reaction size reflects immune sensitisation, not bacterial load. In malnourished or immunocompromised children, Mantoux may actually be falsely negative.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the epidemiology section. The key factors are: age under 5 years, malnutrition, household contact with smear-positive adult, and immature cellular immunity.
Well done. Immature cell-mediated immunity in under-5s, especially combined with malnutrition and household contact, is the key driver of progressive primary TB in this age group.
